'''James Henderson Naismith''' (born 26 July 1968)<ref name="whoswho"/> is a Scot, Professor of [[Structural Biology]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bbsrc.ukri.org/research/grants/grants/PersonDetails.aspx?PersonId=48906|title=Professor James Naismith|website=Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council|access-date=2019-01-25}}</ref>  and since autumn of 2023<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-05-02 |title=James Naismith appointed as Head of MPLS {{!}} University of Oxford |url=https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2023-05-02-james-naismith-appointed-head-mpls |access-date=2023-06-01 |website=www.ox.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> the Head of the [[Divisions of the University of Oxford|Mathematical, Physical, and Life Science Division]] (MPLS) Division at the [[University of Oxford]]. He is also currently Vice-President (non-clinical)<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Vice President (Non-Clinical) announced by Academy |url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/more/news/new-vice-president-non-clinical-announced-by-academy |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=acmedsci.ac.uk}}</ref> of [[Academy of Medical Sciences (United Kingdom)|The Academy of Medical Sciences]] and a Fellow of [[Jesus College, Oxford|Jesus College]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor James Henderson Naismith – Jesus College |url=https://www.jesus.ox.ac.uk/about-jesus-college/our-community/people/professor-james-henderson-naismith/ |access-date=2025-11-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>. He was the acting and inaugural Director (2017-2023) of the [[Rosalind Franklin Institute]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=EPSRC announces interim leadership team for Rosalind Franklin Institute – EPSRC website |url=https://www.epsrc.ac.uk/newsevents/news/rosalindfranklininstituteleadership/ |access-date=2017-08-10 |website=epsrc.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref>  and Director of the Research Complex at [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment|Harwell]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Source |first=Diamond Light |title=Diamond welcomes new Director of the Research Complex at Harwell – Diamond Light Source |url=http://www.diamond.ac.uk/Home/News/LatestNews/2017/23-06-17.html |access-date=2017-08-10 |website=diamond.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> He served as [[Henry Wardlaw|Bishop Wardlaw]] Professor of [[Chemical Biology]] at the [[University of St Andrews]].<ref name="scopus">{{Scopus id}}</ref><ref name="googlescholar">{{Google scholar id}}</ref><ref name="epmc">{{EuropePMC}}</ref><ref name="TathamJaffray2001">{{cite journal |last1=Tatham |first1=Michael H. |last2=Jaffray |first2=Ellis |last3=Vaughan |first3=Owen A. |last4=Desterro |first4=Joana M. P. |last5=Botting |first5=Catherine H. |last6=Naismith |first6=James H. |last7=Hay |first7=Ronald T. |year=2001 |title=Polymeric Chains of SUMO-2 and SUMO-3 Are Conjugated to Protein Substrates by SAE1/SAE2 and Ubc9 |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=276 |issue=38 |pages=35368–35374 |doi=10.1074/jbc.M104214200 |issn=0021-9258 |pmid=11451954 |doi-access=free}}</ref> He was a member of Council of the [[Royal Society]] (2021-2022)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Committees, Working Groups, and Councils {{!}} Royal Society {{!}} Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/sitecore/content/royal-society/configuration/Components/Api2/CommitteeDetailPage/ |access-date=2022-07-12 |website=royalsociety.org}}</ref> and the Vice-Chair of Council (2022-2024) of the [[European XFEL|European X-ray Free Electron Laser]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=XFEL: Federico Boscherini new chair of European XFEL Council |url=https://www.xfel.eu/news_and_events/news/index_eng.html?openDirectAnchor=1968&two_columns=0 |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=www.xfel.eu}}</ref>.

==Education==
Naismith was named after [[James VI and I]]. He was educated at [[Hamilton Grammar School]].<ref name="whoswho"/> He went on to study at the [[University of Edinburgh]] where he received a [[British undergraduate degree classification|first class]] Bachelor of Science degree in [[chemistry]] in 1989. He won a [[Carnegie Trust for the Universities of Scotland|Carnegie Scholarship]] to work under the supervision of Bill Hunter, [[John R. Helliwell]] and [[David Garner (chemist)|David Garner]]<ref name=diamond>{{cite web|url=http://www.diamond.ac.uk/Home/Company/Board/Professor-Jim-Naismith.html|title=Professor Jim Naismith biography |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819090429/http://www.diamond.ac.uk/Home/Company/Board/Professor-Jim-Naismith.html |archive-date=19 August 2014 |publisher=[[Diamond Light Source]]}}</ref><ref name=mib>{{cite web|url=http://www.mib.ac.uk/about/governance/scientificadvisoryboard/|title=Jim Naismith, Scientific Advisory Board|publisher=[[Manchester Institute of Biotechnology]]|access-date=15 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819091340/http://www.mib.ac.uk/about/governance/scientificadvisoryboard/|archive-date=19 August 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> at the [[University of Manchester]] where he received his PhD in 1992<ref name="phd">{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=Jim|last=Naismith |title=Structural studies of Concanavalin A and zinc aldolase |publisher=University of Manchester |year=1992 |url=https://www.librarysearch.manchester.ac.uk/permalink/44MAN_INST/bofker/alma992976153650801631|oclc=1055985285|author-link=Jim Naismith|website=manchester.ac.uk}} {{subscription required}}</ref> for research into the [[chemical structure]] of [[Concanavalin A]] and [[Aldolase|Zinc aldolase]]. In 2016 he was awarded a [[Doctor of Science]] (DSc) by the [[University of St Andrews]].<ref>{{Cite thesis|last=Naismith|first=James H.|date= 2016|title=Structural and chemical studies upon proteins|url=http://library.st-andrews.ac.uk/record=b2411732~S5|publisher=University of St Andrews|degree =DSc|website=st-andrews.ac.uk}}</ref>

==Career and research==
Following his PhD, Naismith did [[postdoctoral research]] at the [[University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center]] as a [[NATO|NATO Fellow]] in the laboratory of Stephen Sprang.<ref name="whoswho"/><ref>{{Cite journal
 | pmid = 8913924
| year = 1995
| last1 = Naismith
| first1 = J. H.
| title = Tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily
| journal = Journal of Inflammation
| volume = 47
| issue = 1–2
| pages = 1–7
| last2 = Sprang
| first2 = S. R.
}}</ref> He was appointed a lecturer at the [[University of St Andrews]] in 1995, [[Reader (academic rank)|Reader]] in 1999 and a Professor in 2001. Naismith's research investigates: {{centred pull quote|The application of [[protein structure]] determination by [[X-ray crystallography]] coupled to [[molecular biology]] and biochemistry to probe biological mechanisms and to target specific [[Biological pathway|disease pathways]]. We have ongoing research in
# [[signal transduction]]
# physical basis of [[Protein–carbohydrate interactions|protein carbohydrate interactions]]
# [[pathogenic bacteria]] [[glycan]] assembly, we have [[Molecular cloning|cloned]] and crystallised a number of the enzymes involved in key steps of glycan synthesis in pathogenic bacteria.
# [[viral replication]], we are purifying and crystallising a [[Protein dimer|heterodimer]] crucial to replication of viruses [[in vivo]],
# the [[biosynthesis]] of unusual [[natural product]]s.<ref>[http://chemistry.st-andrews.ac.uk/staff/jhn/group/ The Naismith Structural Biology Group: Changing the world, one structure at a time…], University of St Andrews</ref>}}

His research has been funded by the [[Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council]] (BBSRC), the [[Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council]] (EPSRC), the [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]] (MRC),<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gtr.rcuk.ac.uk/person/31297C20-181F-473E-923F-6D20BB4ACF09|title=UK Government research grants awarded to James Henderson Naismith|publisher=[[Research Councils UK]]|access-date=15 August 2014|archive-date=19 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819085453/http://gtr.rcuk.ac.uk/person/31297C20-181F-473E-923F-6D20BB4ACF09|url-status=dead}}</ref> the [[Wellcome Trust]] and the [[European Union]].<ref name=wellcome>{{cite web|url=http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/news/archive/2014/title,242061,en.php |title=Major honour for St Andrews scientist Jim Naismith |date=1 May 2014 |publisher=University of St Andrews |archive-date=2014-08-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819090330/http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/news/archive/2014/title,242061,en.php |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Naismith joined the University of Oxford in 2017 as Professor of Structural Biology in the Nuffield Department of Medicine and Senior Research Fellow at [[Jesus College, Oxford|Jesus College]]. He directed the Research Complex at Harwell between 2017 and 2019 and the Rosalind Franklin Institute from 2018.<ref>{{cite web |title=James Naismith appointed as Head of MPLS |url=https://www.ox.ac.uk/news/2023-05-02-james-naismith-appointed-head-mpls |website=University of Oxford |access-date=19 September 2024}}</ref>

===Awards and honours===
Naismith was awarded the 2000 Dextra Carbohydrate award<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carbohydrate Group Awards |url=https://www.rsc.org/membership-and-community/connect-with-others/through-interests/interest-groups/carbohydrate-group/awards/awards/ |access-date=2022-07-12 |website=Royal Society of Chemistry |language=en-GB}}</ref> and the  2009 Jeremy Knowles Prize<ref>{{Cite web |title=Chemistry Biology Interface Division mid-career award: Jeremy Knowles Award - previous winners |url=https://www.rsc.org/prizes-funding/prizes/find-a-prize/chemistry-biology-interface-division-mid-career-award-jeremy-knowles-award/previous-winners/ |access-date=2022-07-12 |website=Royal Society of Chemistry |language=en-GB}}</ref> in Chemical Biology both from the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]. Naismith was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 2014. His nomination reads: {{centred pull quote|Naismith is cited for his stunning structural and chemical dissection of the many proteins involved in natural product recognition, synthesis and export. His work has revealed new paradigms in the recognition of [[nucleic acid]]s and [[carbohydrate]]s, unveiled novel chemical mechanisms for enzymatic [[nucleophilic substitution]] and addition and provided the first views, both structural and dynamic, of [[polysaccharide]] export systems in bacteria. His work is characterised by a synthesis of three-dimensional structural understanding with profound chemical insight.<ref name="royal">{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2014/james-naismith/ |title=Professor James Naismith FMedSci FRS |publisher=royalsociety.org |archive-date=2014-08-13 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140813083722/https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2014/james-naismith/ |location=London |url-status=dead }}</ref>
}}

Naismith was part of the team awarded a 2022 [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] Horizon Prize<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team Nanobodies - 2022 Chemistry Biology Interface Division Horizon Prize: Rita and John Cornforth Award winner |url=https://www.rsc.org/prizes-funding/prizes/2022-winners/team-nanobodies/ |access-date=2022-07-12 |website=Royal Society of Chemistry |language=en-GB}}</ref> for their work on [[Single-domain antibody|nanobodies]] against [[COVID-19|Covid19]]. Naismith is also [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry]] (FRSC), the [[Royal Society of Biology]] (FRSB), the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]] (FRSE), the [[Academy of Medical Sciences, United Kingdom]] (FMedSci), an elected member of the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] (EMBO), in 2016 was elected a [[Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science]] [[American Association for the Advancement of Science|(AAAS)]]<ref>{{cite web|author=Ginger Pinholster |url=http://www.aaas.org/news/2016-aaas-fellows-honored-advancing-science-serve-society |title=2016 AAAS Fellows Honored for Advancing Science to Serve Society &#124; AAAS – The World's Largest General Scientific Society |publisher=AAAS |date=29 November 2016 |access-date=2017-06-07}}</ref> and in 2022 elected a member of Academia Europaea (AE).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Academy of Europe: Naismith James |url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Naismith_James |access-date=2022-07-12 |website=www.ae-info.org}}</ref> His nomination for the Academy of Medical Sciences reads: {{centred pull quote|Jim Naismith is Professor of Chemical Biology at St Andrew's University. He recognised the emerging problem of [[antibiotic resistance]] and has devoted his scientific career to the development of new therapeutic compounds and the identification of novel targets specific to microbial pathogens. Highlights include solving the structure and mechanism of a bacterial fluorinating enzyme, determining the mechanism of [[tryptophan 7-halogenase]] and establishing the structure of an open ''[[Escherichia coli]]'' [[Mechanosensitive channels|mechanosensitive channel]]. His contributions have been recognised by the Carbohydrate Chemistry Medal of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]], the [[Philip Leverhulme Prize|Leverhulme Prize in Molecular Biology]] and the [[Colworth Medal]] of [[Biochemical Society]].<ref name=fmedsci>{{cite web|url=http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/professor-james-naismith/|title=Professor James Naismith FRS FRSE FMedSci|publisher=Academy of Medical Sciences|website=acmedsci.ac.uk|access-date=15 August 2014|archive-date=19 August 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140819085320/http://www.acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/professor-james-naismith/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
}}

==Personal life==
Naismith is married to Rachel Middleton with whom he has one son and one daughter.<ref name="whoswho"/>
